subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage:
"Stop crying, Vaibhav! Be brave!" said Uncle Nikhil at the door of the flat, while Vaibhav, five, sobbed over a torn kite. His mother Indu came in, knelt and said, "It's okay to cry. It's really sad when a kite tears."
Vaibhav sniffed. "I made it myself."
"I know. Come here." She held him for a moment, then asked, "Shall we tell Nani what happened?" "Yes." "And tomorrow we could stick it back together." He wiped his face and nodded.

qa.q: What had torn?
qa.a: Vaibhav's kite had torn.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he said "I made it myself"?
qa.a: He was sad because the kite was something he had worked on, and the tear felt like a real loss. He might also have felt his uncle's words as pressure to hide it.

qa.q: What worked in Indu's response?
qa.a: She said crying was okay, comforted him and then talked about what happened and how to fix it.

qa.q: How might Uncle Nikhil see Vaibhav's crying?
qa.a: He may feel uncomfortable and want to make it stop, without realising that telling Vaibhav to be brave might teach him to hide feelings.

grounding: A child told to be brave may hide feelings, while hearing it's okay to cry helps him handle sadness.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage: Nursery note by Rajni, Class 1 teacher. At pick-up, Jasleen, five, began to cry when her friend left with another girl. The child's aunt said, "Don't cry, be a big girl." Jasleen wiped her eyes hard and went silent. I stayed near her and said, "It's okay to cry, Jasleen. It hurts when a friend leaves." She cried more openly then, and when she was calmer, she said, "I wanted her to stay with me." We talked about asking her friend to play tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the aunt say to Jasleen?
qa.a: She said, "Don't cry, be a big girl."

qa.q: What might Jasleen have felt when she wiped her eyes hard and went silent?
qa.a: She may have felt she was not allowed to be sad, so she tried to hide her feelings. Underneath she was still hurt that her friend left.

qa.q: What could Rajni do to support Jasleen tomorrow?
qa.a: Rajni can help Jasleen ask her friend to play, and keep letting her know that feelings are welcome.

qa.q: How might the aunt see Jasleen's crying?
qa.a: She may think she is helping by telling Jasleen to be big, though this may teach Jasleen to hide her feelings.

grounding: A child told not to cry hides feelings, while comfort and a talk about what happened builds emotional skills.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage: Gautam's speckled hen had gone missing from the coop, and he found feathers by the fence. He burst into tears. Chacha, passing by, said, “Arre, boys don't cry over hens.” Gautam wiped his face hard and swallowed. Gargi Dadi came out and put her arm round him. “It's okay to cry. You loved her.” Gautam cried into her sari. When he was done, Dadi sat with him on the step. “Shall we tell each other what we remember about her?” Gautam sniffed. “She ate from my hand.”

qa.q: What did Gautam find by the fence?
qa.a: Feathers.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he wiped his face hard after Chacha spoke?
qa.a: He was sad about his hen, and ashamed after being told not to cry, so he tried to hide his tears.

qa.q: What did Dadi do after the crying that helps build emotional skills?
qa.a: She comforted him first and then invited him to talk about his memories of the hen.

qa.q: How might Chacha's words and Dadi's words shape Gautam differently?
qa.a: If he listens to Chacha, he may learn to hide feelings; if he listens to Dadi, he learns that crying and talking helps him cope.

grounding: A child told not to cry starts to hide tears, and his grandmother tells him it is okay to cry and talks with him about his hen.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage: Gabriel's best friend moved away from their street in Uppsala on Friday. When the van left, Gabriel's chin wobbled. Anders, his father, said, “Be brave, big boy.” Gabriel turned away and said nothing all evening. At bedtime Anders heard a muffled sniff under the duvet. He sat on the bed. “I was wrong earlier. It's okay to cry. I'd be sad too.” Gabriel threw back the duvet and sobbed. Anders held him. Afterwards they talked about writing a letter to his friend.

qa.q: What did Anders say when the van left?
qa.a: “Be brave, big boy.”

qa.q: Why might Gabriel have turned away and said nothing all evening?
qa.a: He was sad about his friend leaving but felt he had to hide it after being told to be brave.

qa.q: What did Anders do at bedtime that repaired things?
qa.a: He admitted he was wrong, said it was okay to cry, held Gabriel, and then talked about writing a letter.

qa.q: How might Gabriel's friend feel receiving a letter?
qa.a: The friend would likely feel happy and missed, knowing Gabriel was thinking of him.

grounding: A child told to be brave hides his tears, and his father later says it is okay to cry and talks with him.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage: At preschool drop-off, Imran clung to the gate and cried as his father walked away. A boy nearby said, “Crybaby!” Imran hid his face. Farida Miss knelt beside him. “It's okay to cry. It's hard to say bye.” She let him cry on her shoulder. Then she said to the boy, “Everyone cries sometimes. We're kind to friends who are sad.” After a few minutes, Imran wiped his eyes. Farida asked, “What would help you feel better?” He pointed at the water table.

qa.q: What did the boy nearby say?
qa.a: “Crybaby!”

qa.q: Why did Imran hide his face after the boy spoke?
qa.a: He was sad about his father leaving and embarrassed at being called a crybaby.

qa.q: What did Farida Miss do that builds emotional skills?
qa.a: She said it was okay to cry, comforted him, and then asked what would help him feel better.

qa.q: How might the boy who said “crybaby” see crying after Farida spoke?
qa.a: He might start to see crying as normal and learn to be kinder to sad friends.

grounding: A child crying at drop-off is teased, and his teacher shows that it is okay to cry and helps him recover.

subtype: Learning it is okay to cry [Regulating]
passage:
I'm Nilesh, Jagdish's cousin from the next house. On Sunday his new cricket bat cracked down the middle. His face crumpled and tears started.

"Boys don't cry. Be brave," his uncle said. Jagdish swallowed hard, went stiff and walked away. He didn't talk for the rest of the match.

That evening his grandmother found him on the steps. "It's okay to cry, beta. That bat was special." He cried into her shoulder for a long time.

Afterwards they talked about fixing it with tape. He even smiled.

qa.q: What happened to Jagdish's new cricket bat?
qa.a: It cracked down the middle.

qa.q: What was Jagdish probably feeling when he swallowed hard and walked away?
qa.a: He was most likely very sad about the bat and also ashamed after being told not to cry, so he hid his feelings. Going stiff and silent suggests he was holding them in.

qa.q: Which response helped Jagdish more, and why?
qa.a: His grandmother's did: saying it was okay to cry, comforting him, then talking about fixing the bat helped him get through the sadness.

qa.q: What would change if the uncle's words were the only response Jagdish heard?
qa.a: He might learn to hide his sadness every time, staying stiff and silent instead of getting comfort and help.

grounding: It shows a child told not to cry hiding his feelings, then comforted and told it is okay to cry, followed by a talk about what happened.
